overview: The Bagrationi rulers brought together a Georgian kingdom in 1008, followed by an influential medieval monarchy in the Caucasus. This card follows that united kingdom and its later fragmentation. The imported map’s approximate 1000-1530 span begins before unification and continues after the kingdom divided. Its changing outlines are broad snapshots, not precise frontiers or a claim that every community within them had the same language and identity.

periods.title: A united monarchy
periods.summary: Bagrat III’s unification established the kingdom whose later rulers expanded royal power.

periods.title: Royal power and cultural achievement
periods.summary: David IV and Tamar’s era brought ambitious foundations, learning and artistic patronage.

periods.title: Invasion, recovery and fragmentation
periods.summary: Mongol invasions began in the 1220s. Later recoveries did not prevent eventual division into regional states; 1490 here marks the late-fifteenth-century transition approximately.

periods.title: Separate Georgian states
periods.summary: The atlas continues across a period of separate kingdoms and principalities, with growing Ottoman and Safavid pressure.

sections.title: A kingdom built through people and institutions

items.text: David IV became king in 1089 after his father abdicated. He strengthened royal authority against rebellious nobles and reorganized the church at the Ruisi-Urbnisi council of 1103. Governing a kingdom meant negotiating and sometimes confronting powerful landholders and religious leaders, as well as winning battles.

A copper coin associated with David shows him in Byzantine imperial clothing but leaves out the subordinate Byzantine titles used on earlier money. Its Georgian inscription lists several peoples over whom he claimed kingship, including Abkhazians, Kartvelians and Armenians. A small object could advertise very large political ambitions.

Tamar’s royal portraits carefully presented her place in the dynasty. At Vardzia she appears beside her father, Giorgi III; another surviving portrait groups her with her husband and heir. These church paintings helped make a woman’s royal authority visible through family, costume and sacred setting.

David founded Gelati Monastery near Kutaisi in 1106. Its builders fitted carefully cut stone into a monumental church, completed under his son Demetre in 1130. A twelfth-century mosaic shows the Virgin and Child between archangels. Building, carving and laying coloured mosaic pieces required different kinds of skilled hands.

Gelati’s academy connected Georgian readers with Greek philosophy. Ioane Petritzi translated Proclus, while Arsen Ikaltoeli compiled the Dogmatikon, a collection influenced by Aristotle. This was advanced scholarly learning at a particular institution; the surviving evidence does not establish that every child attended school.

A twelfth-century Gospel associated with Gelati preserves its work as a centre for copying and decorating books. The monastery’s scriptorium has not been located, but the manuscript survives in the National Centre of Manuscripts. Sometimes the book lasts even when the room where it was made is lost.

At Vardzia, monks and builders cut a multilevel monastery into the rock during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The wider Vardzia-Khertvisi gorge preserves cave dwellings, cells and shared buildings. Their surviving interiors help researchers study room arrangements that have disappeared from many ordinary buildings above ground.

The same gorge was a working landscape. Villages and arable plots occupied terraces that followed the steep terrain, while fortresses and churches stood on prominent heights. Food production and everyday settlement belonged beside the famous monuments, even when the cliffside monastery attracts most of the photographs.

sections.title: Bathhouses, workshops and a winter hearth

items.text: Excavations at medieval Dmanisi uncovered paved streets, bathhouses, barns and wine cellars. Together these remains reveal a town where people stored food, moved goods and maintained places for bathing. They give a more practical picture of urban life than a list of royal victories can provide.

Dmanisi’s craftspeople made pottery and glass. Excavated objects also include tools and ornaments of bone, stone and metal. Producing containers, working materials and decorating bodies helped sustain the town’s economy. Medieval shoppers needed useful things to put on shelves as well as beautiful things to wear.

Archaeologists also identified a mosque and a madrasa, an institution of Islamic learning, at Dmanisi. Their presence helps show why the Georgian kingdom cannot be reduced to a single religious experience. A Christian monarchy governed towns containing different institutions and communities.

In the surviving Svan house tradition of medieval origin, people and livestock shared the ground floor, separated by a wooden partition. An open hearth warmed the hall, and a corridor helped insulate it. This is a regional mountain-house tradition, not a plan for every Georgian home. Winter housemates could have hooves.

The upper storey of these Svan houses served as summer living space and storage for fodder and tools. A doorway connected the house to its tower. Seasonal arrangements joined family life, farming supplies and protection within one building complex, rather than assigning each task a separate modern-style room.

sections.title: A doctor’s book and a king’s name

items.text: A medical text survives beneath later writing in manuscript S 4939. Specialists date its lower layer to the thirteenth century from the handwriting. Its fragments discuss blood, kidneys, foods, vegetables and fruit. Reused parchment preserved traces of how medieval writers connected diet with the body.

Zaza of Panaskerti’s fifteenth-century Medical Book, preserved as Q 877, gathers earlier medical learning and remedies. Its opening section discusses matters including hygiene, examining a patient and preparing medicines; later sections address particular organs and their diseases. The book records historical approaches to care, not instructions to follow today.

An early-thirteenth-century copper coin of Giorgi IV carries the Georgian legend “ႢႨႻႤ / ႧႫႰႱႠ”, translated by the university catalogue as “Giorgi, son of Tamar.” These are abbreviated Asomtavruli letters, with the slash marking a line break. The surrounding inscription carries the calendar date equivalent to 1210; Arabic and Persian legends appear on the other side.

Many coins of this era were irregular copper pieces rather than tidy circles. Parts of a design could miss the edge altogether. Scholars have suggested that such money was weighed in transactions. Giorgi’s coin even calls itself silver in its legend despite being copper: the wording and the metal tell different parts of its monetary history.

sections.title: The kingdom divided; its communities continued

items.text: Mongol invasions from the 1220s disrupted the kingdom. Periods of recovery followed, but by the end of the fifteenth century political authority was divided among Kartli, Kakheti, Imereti and Samtskhe-Saatabago. The history is a sequence of invasions, recoveries and regional rulers, not one uninterrupted collapse.

ending.text: The united kingdom fragmented into regional states by the late fifteenth century. Georgian communities, languages, churches, books and ruling families continued. The imported 1530 endpoint falls within this later political landscape, as Ottoman and Safavid competition intensified; it is not a date when Georgia or its people disappeared.
